summary.text: Elder son of Lelex, the aboriginal first king of Laconia, and the second to reign over the Leleges; on his father's death the kingdom passed to him, his younger brother Polycaon remaining a private man. From Myles the line ran to his son Eurotas and the river that bears that name.

story.text: In the deep antiquity of Laconia, Pausanias says, Lelex an aboriginal was the first king, and after him the people were called Leleges. Lelex had a son Myles and a younger one, Polycaon; and when Lelex died, Myles as the elder received the kingdom, while Polycaon, being the younger, remained a private person until he married Messene and a foreign throne carried him off elsewhere. So Myles stands second in the oldest royal line the land remembers.

His very name carries his deed. At a place called Alesiae, the Place of Grinding, on the road toward Taygetus, the Lacedaemonians said that Myles the son of Lelex — Myles meaning Mill-man — was the first human being to invent a mill, and that it was here he ground his corn. The tale survives in Pausanias alone, a king reckoned not by conquest but by the founding gift of bread.

On the death of Myles his son Eurotas succeeded to the throne; and it was Eurotas who drained the standing water of the plain down to the sea by a trench and gave his name to the river left behind. Through his daughter Sparta, wedded to Lacedaemon, the founding house of Laconia descended onward from the miller-king. Pausanias adds that the Spartans kept hero-shrines from this age — of Lelex himself, and of one Iops said to have been born in the time of Lelex or of Myles.
